readerTitle: Two managers asked for a yes. Only one kept the boss's trust.
caseNote: 가상 사례 2개 (부품 창고의 운송사 교체, 소프트웨어 회사의 장애 대응 계획) · 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 제안의 설득력은 장점을 늘어놓는 데서가 아니라, 그 선택이 무엇을 포기하는지 먼저 말하는 데서 나온다.
misconception: 단점을 말하면 제안이 약해 보이니 장점만 강조해야 승인받는다. 또는 선택지를 공정하게 나열만 하고 결정은 윗사람에게 맡기는 것이 정직하다.

sources.text: 의사결정 커뮤니케이션의 일반 원칙 (선택지별 이득과 비용 제시, 권고안 명시)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 창고 사례의 연 $40,000 절감, 배송 1일 지연, 소프트웨어 사례의 1분기 전면 재구축 대 2분기 단계적 계획은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계나 연구를 인용하지 않았습니다.
5번 카드의 5가지 항목(선택지, 이득, 비용, 권고, 판단을 바꿀 신호)은 특정 프레임워크가 아니라 일반적인 정리 방식으로 썼습니다. 특정 기업이나 저자의 방식으로 소개하지 않았는지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Two managers asked for a yes. Only one kept the boss's trust.
body: A warehouse manager and a software product lead each brought a big proposal to their boss in the same month. Both got approved.
Two months later, one boss felt misled. The other felt like a partner. The difference wasn't the idea. It was whether they said out loud what the idea would cost.

image.label: Two people presenting to two bosses, one with a hidden note
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 구성. 왼쪽은 창고 배경에서 관리자가 "Save $40K"만 적힌 보드를 들고 있고, 등 뒤에 작은 쪽지가 숨겨져 있음. 오른쪽은 사무실에서 제품 책임자가 "Gain / Cost" 두 칸이 보이는 보드를 펼쳐 보임. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: Cheaper freight, slower trucks.
body: You run a parts warehouse. A regional carrier would save about $40,000 a year, but deliveries to some customers would take one extra day.
You think the switch is worth it. How do you pitch it to the operations director?

options.text: Lead with the $40,000 saving. The extra day is minor, so save it for questions.
options.feedback: You get a quick yes, but the director approves a deal they don't fully understand. When a customer complains about the extra day, your credibility pays for it.

options.text: Lay out three carrier options with pros and cons, and let the director choose.
options.feedback: Honest and complete, but you've handed over the thinking. The director wants your judgment, not just a menu.

options.text: Recommend the switch, say plainly it adds a day for some customers, and show the option you rejected.
options.feedback: The director sees the price of the saving and can weigh it. If they disagree, you find out now, not after the contract is signed.

cards.title: Same kind of request, different endings.
body: Dana, the warehouse manager, pitched only the saving. Approved in ten minutes. Then a large customer who restocked weekly complained about late parts. The director asked why nobody had mentioned it.

Leo, a product lead at a software company, asked to pause new features for six weeks to fix outages. He named the cost: two sales demos would slip. The CEO pushed back, and they agreed to keep one demo on track. **The plan changed a little. Trust didn't.**

cards.title: Presenting trade-offs
body: **Presenting trade-offs** means showing what each real option gains and what it gives up, then saying which cost you recommend accepting and why.

Every decision has a price. When you hide it, the decision-maker discovers it later and blames you. When you name it, they can judge whether the price is worth paying, and they trust the rest of your numbers more.

image.label: A balance scale with gains on one side and costs on the other
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일 저울. 한쪽 접시에 "What we gain" 블록, 다른 쪽에 "What we give up" 블록이 같은 크기로 올라가 있고, 저울 위에 "My pick" 깃발이 꽂혀 있음. 로고 없음.

cards.title: A trade-off pitch answers five questions.
body: It fits on one page, and both Leo's pitch and a better version of Dana's would cover the same ground:
list: **Options:** two or three real choices, including doing nothing
**Costs:** what each one gives up, in plain terms
**Pick:** your recommendation and the cost you accept
cards.callout: The cost line is the one people most often skip.

cards.title: It brings different values into the open.
body: Dana's director didn't disagree with the math. She cared more about one big customer than Dana did. That isn't a fact Dana could look up. It's a judgment about what matters.

Naming the trade-off surfaces those judgments while you can still adjust. The same holds when options look equal, like two suppliers or two hires. The choice is rarely about which is better. It's about **which weakness you can live with**.

cards.title: Fake balance is worse than none.
body: Some pitches show a "trade-off" where one option is obviously weak, set up only to lose. People notice, and it reads as a sales trick.
Two other traps: too many options, which buries the decision, and so many caveats that your recommendation disappears. Show the real costs, then still **lead with your answer**.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You lead product at a software business. Frequent outages are hurting renewals. A full rebuild of the database layer would fix it but tie up the whole team for one quarter. A phased plan would take two quarters but keep some feature work going.
Which pitch to the CEO is strongest?

options.text: Recommend the full rebuild. Say it freezes new features for a quarter, and show the phased plan as the alternative.
options.feedback: The CEO sees both real paths and the price of yours. They can push back on the freeze now, instead of finding out when sales asks where the features went.

options.text: Recommend the full rebuild and focus on how much more stable the product will be.
options.feedback: Persuasive in the room. But the feature freeze is the cost everyone will feel, and leaving it out makes the pitch look like it was hiding something.

options.text: Present both plans with their costs, and ask the CEO to pick.
options.feedback: Fair and clear, but you know the details best. Without your pick, the CEO has to rebuild your reasoning from scratch.

cards.title: Every recommendation has a price. Say it out loud.
body: When you name what your choice gives up, people can weigh it, push back early, and trust the rest of what you say.
**Try it today:** take a proposal you're about to make. Add one line, "What we give up:", and fill it in honestly.
